text: I want to argue that multitasking, at least in the cognitively demanding sense most people mean, is largely a myth rather than a skill worth cultivating. In my own experience as a graduate student, the moments I felt most "productive" while juggling reading, email, and a half-written draft were precisely the moments my work was thinnest. What actually happens is not parallel processing but rapid switching, and that switching carries a measurable cost. When people attempt to perform two or more related tasks either at the same time or alternating rapidly between them, errors go up substantially, and it takes far longer to get the tasks done than if they were done sequentially. That tradeoff rarely shows up in the moment, because the feeling of busyness masks the underlying inefficiency.The stronger objection is that what we praise as multitasking skill is usually just task-switching that has been practiced enough to feel smooth. A nurse or an air-traffic controller is not literally attending to ten things at once; they have built routines that let them sample and reprioritize quickly. Cultivating that kind of disciplined attention seems far more valuable than chasing the fantasy of doing everything simultaneously. If anything, the skill worth developing is the opposite of multitasking: protecting a single line of deep work long enough for it to amount to something.
